\title{HARE: High-Throughput Authenticated Encryption\\
for RISC-V GPGPUs via an ISE}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Anonymous authors}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Paper under double-blind review}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Authenticated encryption (AEAD) now guards every path data takes between
devices, and GPGPUs increasingly produce and consume that data---yet the GPU
is the one place the AEAD itself cannot run cheaply. Software AES-GCM costs
70.9 cycles per byte on our platform, and fixed-function engines freeze the
algorithm at tape-out and sit outside the programming model.
This paper presents HARE, a systematic study of the instruction-set-extension
design space for AEAD on SIMT GPGPUs. We organize the space into four tiers
by where the cipher's block state lives---S0 software, S1 lane-local
instructions, S2 stateful engines, S3 subgroup-cooperative instructions---and
implement AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 at every tier in the RTL of an
open-source RISC-V GPGPU. Measurement under balanced two-core execution
yields three results. First, the two algorithms harvest at different tiers:
lane-local instructions, the SIMT analogue of the ratified scalar
cryptography extensions, deliver $14.6$--$18.2\times$ for AES-GCM but only
$1.55\times$ for ChaCha20-Poly1305. Second, subgroup-cooperative
instructions carry the lowest marginal cost for both algorithms once the
subgroup and the instruction's granularity span the cipher's block state:
four lanes for AES's 128-bit state ($4.92\times$ over lane-local), sixteen
for ChaCha's 512-bit state ($4.32\times$ large-footprint and $8.41\times$
small-footprint, where a four-lane form returns $1.29\times$); the
sixteen-lane form ties the stateful engine large-footprint, leads
$1.61\times$ small-footprint, and carries no persistent context---at the
price of start-up the engine's context exists to amortize. Third, state \emph{inside one
instruction's execution} occupies an
interior optimum between stateless instructions, which bottleneck on issue
bandwidth ($1.78\times$ slower), and architectural context, which costs
$2.9\times$ the area plus key-lifetime semantics. All designs close timing
at 200\,MHz on a Stratix~10 FPGA; the recommended ChaCha pair adds 3.4\% to
the core it extends. End to end, HARE reaches $72\times$ (AES-GCM) and
$6.6\times$ (ChaCha20-Poly1305) over software.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

Data in flight is now encrypted by default, and almost all of it under one of
two authenticated ciphers: AES-GCM~\cite{sp800-38d,mcgrew2004gcm} and
ChaCha20-Poly1305~\cite{rfc8439} carry TLS~1.3, QUIC, disk and object
storage, and---most recently---the secured CPU--GPU and GPU--GPU links of
confidential accelerators~\cite{nvidia-h100-cc,lee2025gputee}. Over the same
decade, GPGPUs have become the place where this data is produced and
consumed. The two trends meet badly: the machine that touches the data is
the one machine that cannot afford to encrypt it.

A SIMT core today has two options. It can run the AEAD in software over the
base ISA: on the open-source Vortex GPGPU~\cite{tine2021vortex} we measure
70.9 cycles per byte (\cB) for AES-GCM---and the fast software AES it uses,
T-tables, is also the canonical cache-timing victim. Or the system can bolt
on a fixed-function engine: fast, but frozen at tape-out, reachable only by
DMA round-trip, and closed to every algorithm chosen after silicon. CPUs
resolved this same tension a decade ago with ISA extensions---AES-NI on
x86~\cite{gueron2010aesni}, and for RISC-V the ratified scalar
(Zkn/Zbc)~\cite{riscv-scalar-crypto} and vector (Zvk)~\cite{riscv-vector-crypto}
cryptography extensions. Inside a SIMT pipeline, the corresponding design
space is essentially unexplored.

Exploring it produces two surprises. The obvious first step is to port the
scalar extensions into every lane. This helps unevenly: it buys AES-GCM
$18.2\times$ at the small-footprint point ($14.6\times$ large-footprint),
because it deletes the table lookups, but ChaCha20-Poly1305
only $1.55\times$, because ARX rounds were never table-bound---the
correct-by-construction port of the ratified extensions leaves the second
cipher almost untouched. The obvious second step is a stateful engine: write
the key once into hardware context, then stream blocks through it. It
works---$1.81\times$ and $4.09\times$ over the lane-local tier---but it is
the most expensive point in the space (+112{,}951 ALMs on a 183{,}971-ALM
core for ChaCha20-Poly1305), and it plants per-(warp,\,lane) key material in the
pipeline, with the zeroize-on-ownership-change and save-or-destroy-on-%
preemption semantics resident secrets drag behind them---and on both
algorithms, at both operating points, it is not the lowest-cost tier.

HARE's answer is a third structure and two design rules. In the
\emph{subgroup-cooperative} tier, the cipher's block state never leaves the
register file: it lies spread one 32-bit word per lane across an aligned
group of lanes, and a single instruction reads that group's registers with
fixed routing and advances an entire round---or absorbs an entire block.
No architectural state exists anywhere. The first rule is that the
subgroup---and the granularity of what one instruction advances---must span
the cipher's block state: AES's 128-bit state is four lanes wide and a
four-lane form returns $4.92\times$; ChaCha's 512-bit state is sixteen
lanes wide, and the same four-lane structure that serves AES returns
$1.29\times$ where a sixteen-lane, round-granular form returns $4.32\times$
($8.41\times$ small-footprint). The second rule
concerns the state a multi-cycle instruction holds \emph{while it executes}:
none at all bottlenecks on issue bandwidth ($1.78\times$ slower), and full
architectural context pays $2.9\times$ the area and the lifetime semantics;
1{,}154 bits of instruction-internal working registers---the interior
point---beats both ends.

This paper contributes:
\begin{itemize}
\item a design-space taxonomy (S0--S3) for AEAD ISEs in SIMT pipelines,
  organized by where the cipher's block state lives, with every tier
  implemented for two AEADs in the RTL of an open-source RISC-V GPGPU and
  verified against NIST and RFC test vectors in two independent models;
\item the measurement that the two AEADs harvest at different tiers, and
  that the subgroup-cooperative tier has the lowest marginal cost for
  both---$4.92\times$ and $4.32\times$ over lane-local at the large-footprint
  point, $5.81\times$ and $8.41\times$ small-footprint, $72\times$ and
  $6.6\times$ over software---while, for ChaCha, staying essentially tied
  with the stateful engine large-footprint and $1.61\times$ ahead
  small-footprint with no persistent context;
\item the width-and-granularity rule, with the $1.29\times{\to}4.32\times$
  inversion that follows from matching the subgroup and the instruction's
  granularity to the block state; and
\item the state-placement result: an interior optimum between stateless
  and stateful designs, with the issue-bandwidth mechanism that explains
  it---plus the engineering result that every subgroup instruction fits
  standard two-read-one-write operand delivery, and the extension's one
  three-source instruction rides an operand path the base machine already
  had.
\end{itemize}

All measurements derive from a committed, gated, per-run measurement record
taken with both cores verifiably busy, and from archived place-and-route
reports; every design closes timing at 200\,MHz on a Stratix~10 FPGA.

\section{Background}\label{sec:background}

\subsection{SIMT execution and subgroups}
A SIMT core executes \emph{warps}; each warp issues one instruction over
$k$ \emph{lanes} (here $k{=}16$), and each lane owns a private scalar
register file. A \emph{subgroup} is an aligned group of lanes within one
warp (lanes $4q..4q{+}3$ for width four; all sixteen for width sixteen).
Vortex~\cite{tine2021vortex} is an open-source RISC-V GPGPU with this
organization; our configuration is two cores, four warps per core, sixteen
lanes per warp, RV32IM.

\subsection{Two AEADs, by state size}
AES-GCM encrypts 16-byte blocks through 10--14 rounds over a
\textbf{128-bit} state and authenticates with GHASH, a multiply in
GF($2^{128}$)~\cite{sp800-38d}. ChaCha20 keeps a \textbf{512-bit} state of
sixteen 32-bit words; a double round applies eight add-xor-rotate (ARX)
quarter-round lines across columns and then diagonals~\cite{bernstein2008chacha}.
Poly1305 absorbs 16-byte blocks into a 130-bit accumulator held as five
26-bit limbs~\cite{bernstein2005poly}. Two numbers in this paragraph do all
the work in Section~\ref{sec:eval}: $128 = 4\times$ a 32-bit lane, and
$512 = 16\times$.

\section{The design space: where the state lives}\label{sec:space}

We organize AEAD ISEs for SIMT machines into four tiers
(Fig.~\ref{fig:tiers}), distinguished by a single question: \emph{where does
the cipher's block state live, and what may one instruction read?}

\textbf{S0 --- software.} State lives in per-lane registers and memory; an
instruction reads two registers of one lane. Every state move and table
lookup is explicit.

\textbf{S1 --- lane-local.} Same state residence; an instruction now
performs a cipher \emph{step}---a T-less AES round step, a carry-less
multiply, an xor-rotate, a 26-bit MAC---but still sees one lane's two
operands: the SIMT port of the ratified scalar
extensions~\cite{riscv-scalar-crypto}.

\textbf{S2 --- stateful engine.} State moves out of the register file into
unit-private \emph{architectural context}, addressed by (warp,\,lane).
Context writes load key and nonce once; per-block instructions reference
the context implicitly, so the stream shrinks to data in, data out. The
context survives between instructions---which is precisely this tier's
cost: storage for every (warp,\,lane) plus a lifetime of ownership,
validity, and zeroization.

\textbf{S3 --- subgroup-cooperative.} State returns to the register file,
but spread one word per lane across an aligned subgroup; a single
instruction reads the subgroup's operand vector with \emph{fixed} lane
routing (no crossbar) and writes one result per lane. Nothing survives the
instruction. S2 changes where state lives; S3 changes only \emph{who may
read it}.

Three properties frame everything that follows. All instructions of tiers
S1--S3 have fixed, data-independent latency and no data-dependent memory
access, so every hardware tier is constant-time by construction---unlike the
T-table software they replace. Subgroup instructions require their subgroup
fully converged (the mask must cover all lanes of the group; both our models
assert it). And only S2 creates resident secrets: S1 and S3 leave nothing in the pipeline for a context switch to
leak---for confidential deployments, ``no resident secrets'' is an
argument of the recommended tier, not a side effect.

\section{The HARE instructions}\label{sec:ise}

Table~\ref{tab:isa} lists every instruction in the extension. Three format
facts frame it. The only three-source instruction is the S1
multiply-accumulate family, which is R4-type and rides the operand path the
base machine already provides for its gather instruction---no read port is
added anywhere. Every subgroup-cooperative instruction is plain 2R1W. And
the engines' streaming operations write \texttt{x0}, so they produce no
scoreboard entry at all: ordering comes from the unit itself, which stalls
issue while busy.

\subsection{S1: the ratified vocabulary, in every lane}
The measured AES-GCM S1 row uses five \emph{ratified} instructions and
nothing else: \texttt{aes32esi}/\texttt{aes32esmi} (Zkne) compute one byte's
round step, and \texttt{clmul}/\texttt{clmulh} (Zbkc) with \texttt{brev8}
(Zbkb) build GHASH in the reflected domain, the accumulator and hash subkey
living in ordinary registers. We additionally built a custom reduction pair
(\texttt{ghred32l/h}) and measured it: it raises load traffic and does not
pay, so the row does not use it. The tier's $18.2\times$ is therefore
available to any RV32 SIMT machine that simply adopts the existing scalar
extensions in its lanes---which is precisely why we treat S1 as the
baseline for novelty, not as a contribution.

ChaCha20-Poly1305 has no ratified equivalent, so its S1 is two custom
instructions. \texttt{chacha32.xr} fuses the XOR and left-rotate that end
every ARX line, turning a three-instruction line into two---and buys almost
nothing ($1.09\times$ alone), because the line's add remains and the round
count is untouched. \texttt{poly26.mac} is the instruction that matters: a
26-bit limb multiply-accumulate whose low/high split is exact rather than
approximate (the low form accumulates products mod $2^{26}$, the high form
their quotients), R4-type on the machine's existing three-source path.

\subsection{S2: stateful engines}
Context-write instructions (\texttt{.cwr}) load key material into
unit-private storage addressed by (warp,\,lane); streaming instructions then
advance whole rounds or blocks against it. Three folds keep the streams
short. The AES engine runs its key schedule \emph{on the fly}
(\texttt{aes.rndm} computes $\mathrm{NextKey}$ as it rounds, so no expanded
schedule is ever stored or loaded); \texttt{ghash.cwr} XORs the incoming
block into the accumulator as it writes, absorbing for free; and
\texttt{chacha.begin} rebuilds the whole 512-bit initial state from one
counter operand, so after the once-per-message key write \emph{a ChaCha
block costs no context writes at all}, and \texttt{chacha.crd} folds the
feed-forward add into the read. The ChaCha context is 896 bits per
(warp,\,lane)---512 state, 256 key, 96 nonce, 32 counter---which at four
warps and sixteen lanes is 57{,}344 bits per core; its register cost is
predictable from that definition. Context is per lane, not
per warp, by design: sharing one key per warp was rejected because batching
records from \emph{different} sessions---different keys in the same
warp---is the case that makes a GPU worth using for AEAD at all.
There is deliberately no Poly1305 engine: five limbs live in ten
registers and a block step is ten three-source MACs, so the ChaCha-Poly
S2 row pairs its cipher engine with the lane-local \texttt{poly26.mac};
GHASH's full GF($2^{128}$) block step is where a stateful authenticator
pays, which is why only the AES-GCM S2 row is a dual engine.

\subsection{S3: subgroup-cooperative instructions}
For AES-GCM the subgroup is an aligned quad: lane $i$ holds column $i$ of
the 128-bit state, \texttt{aesrm.sg4}/\texttt{aesrf.sg4} perform a complete
round each (the ShiftRows lane exchange is fixed wiring), and
\texttt{ghmul.sg4} a full GF($2^{128}$) multiply, at the price of four
carry-less multipliers per lane where the lane-local path needs one---the
area consequence appears in Table~\ref{tab:area}.

ChaCha gets the same four-lane treatment as a control:
\texttt{chacha32.xr}'s route bit reads \texttt{rs2} from the next lane,
\texttt{chadd.sg4} adds across the quad, and \texttt{poly26.rsum.sg4} folds
the four per-lane Poly1305 partial sums into every lane at once. These are
real instructions that win real cycles over S1---and
Fig.~\ref{fig:width} shows the whole four-lane package is the wrong width
for a 512-bit state.

At sixteen lanes, lane $i$ holds word $i$ and \texttt{chacha.dr.sg16}
advances one full double round per instruction---ten per block. It executes
as a fixed ten-cycle sequence over 1{,}154 bits of working registers,
owner-locked while in flight; nothing survives the instruction.
\texttt{poly4.step.sg16} absorbs a whole 64-byte ChaCha block---four
Poly1305 blocks---in one instruction: the accumulator $h$ travels in lanes
0--4, the key $r$ in lanes 5--9 of the \emph{same} source register, and the
result returns $h'$ with $r$ untouched, so the output feeds the next absorb
directly. The $r^2,r^3,r^4$ schedule that block-parallel software Poly1305
must hold in registers (we measure it at 20 loads per block and 36\% of
kernel cycles) exists only inside the unit, and never becomes architectural.

\subsection{Encoding}
Packing $h$ and $r$ into one operand is what keeps the sixteen-lane tier
2R1W: the first version of \texttt{poly4.step.sg16} read them from two
registers---five lanes used, eleven dead, in each---and needed an R4-type
third source for the message. Ten of sixteen lanes carry both values with
six to spare; the repack costs +218 ALMs and 17 instructions per message
(under 2\% of cycles), and returns a seven-bit funct7 where R4 offers
two. One caution generalizes: our four-bit sub-opcode space filled
completely---the sixteen-lane double round, its stateless ablation, and
the S2 round op share one slot (the build refuses any two together)---so
budget opcode space as deliberately as area.

\section{Methodology}\label{sec:method}

All cycle counts come from Verilator simulation of the synthesized RTL
configuration (two cores $\times$ four warps $\times$ sixteen lanes) with a
DDR4 model; instruction counts from an independent functional simulator that
agrees with the RTL to the instruction. Both models pass the NIST GCM and
RFC~8439 test vectors for every implementation at every tier. Simulation is
deterministic---repeated runs are byte-identical---so every difference we
report is a design difference, not noise.

A recorded run must exit cleanly, verify its AEAD outputs, and produce
exactly one measurement record carrying the per-core retired-instruction
split. All figures use 128 messages---the smallest count, by saturation
sweep, at which every implementation keeps both cores evenly busy
(min/max split $\ge 0.99$ in every row); below it a lane-mapped kernel
idles the second core, and a lane-vs-subgroup ratio compares one active
core against two. Per-byte figures are three-point marginal fits with an
intercept per regime: small-footprint over 4--16\,KiB (AES-GCM) and
8--32\,KiB (ChaCha-Poly) of payload, large-footprint over the \emph{same}
128--512\,KiB and 1--4\,KiB record lengths for both algorithms, every
point at a power-of-two blocks count---measured, not stylistic:
non-power-of-two counts give non-power-of-two strides, and the dataset's
diagnostic rows put lane and engine tiers 7--25\% off the line there
(subgroup tiers ${\sim}1\%$). Table generation aborts unless each
three-point slope agrees with its two-point pair within 5\%; the S0 and
SG4 rows keep flat two-point pairs, and the S3/16 small fit keeps its
endpoint pair (at 8.6k cycles of per-message start-up, payload is 2\% of
a small run, so a third point adds estimator noise). The points are named
by footprint, not cache residency: counters show both are DRAM-dominated
(36--320 DRAM bytes moved per payload byte, 260--740 cycles per request)
and differ in amplification and start-up share. Fits never mix builds;
subgroup rows divide by an anchor from the same build, and re-measuring
anchors and subgroup forms in the one combined build that carries the
whole extension reproduces three slopes bit-identically, the fourth
within 1.5\%. Marginal fits cancel per-message start-up, so
Sec.~\ref{sec:eval} also reports whole-run figures where it is paid;
per-message costs are priced at setup-light points (at a 64-message grid,
three quarters of a short run is setup, and the operand repack of
Sec.~\ref{sec:ise}-D reads 3--6\% there against its true ${<}2\%$). All
kernels implement the AEAD \emph{sealing} path---plaintext in, ciphertext
and tag out; device-side opening is not implemented and no claim covers
it.
Area and timing come from Quartus place-and-route for
a DE10-Pro (Stratix~10 1SG280HU1F50E1VG) with a 200\,MHz GPU clock; we
report a build only if its GPU clock domain closes in every one of the 30
timing-model/corner entries. The frozen per-run dataset (48 gated rows,
one tagged commit), the RTL, and the place-and-route reports accompany the
paper.

and speedups against each algorithm's own S1 measured in the same build.
$\Delta$ALM is the whole build against the crypto-free core (183{,}971
ALMs); each build includes its lane-local parent units.}

\subsection{Different algorithms harvest at different tiers}
Table~\ref{tab:tiers} is the paper's central measurement. Reading the
large-footprint $\times$S1 column: AES-GCM's big step is S0${\to}$S1
(up to $18.2\times$)---the
tier that deletes its table lookups---after which the stateful engine adds
$1.81\times$ and the subgroup form $4.92\times$. ChaCha's S1 buys only
$1.55\times$: ARX was never table-bound, and its costs sit in the sheer
count of round operations, which only round-level instructions (S2/S3)
remove. The design consequence: a GPGPU that stops at the ported scalar
extensions has solved AES and left ChaCha almost untouched; one that stops
at stateful engines has paid the most area for neither algorithm's best row.
The per-step pattern falls out of the $\times$S1 columns: AES-GCM's
largest step is the first, ChaCha's is the second, and the subgroup step
multiplies both at the small-footprint point ($1.49\times$,
$1.61\times$); at the large-footprint point it is decisive for AES-GCM
($2.71\times$) and, for ChaCha, a narrow win ($1.05\times$) whose real
argument is what it does \emph{not} cost---S2's context and its lifetime.
HARE-SG16 achieves the lowest observed marginal cost in both regimes:
essentially tied with S2 in the large-footprint regime (1.728 against
1.807\,\cB) and $1.61\times$ ahead small-footprint, while avoiding
persistent architectural crypto context. The ChaCha S2 row has no
Poly1305 engine (Sec.~\ref{sec:ise}-B) and 42\% of its instructions are
the lane-local authenticator---so we measured the missing engine's
ceiling: a diagnostic that deletes every absorb (83\% of the stream) runs
5\% \emph{slower} (1.890 against 1.807\,\cB). The MACs execute in the
shadow of the engine's eight-cycle double-rounds, a zero-instruction
authenticator would buy nothing, and the tie stands.
One definitional note: the ChaCha S0 row
assumes rotate instructions (Zbb semantics); without them the large-footprint
figure moves only 2.4\%---both variants are bound by the same memory
system---so the ladder does not hinge on that choice.
At both operating points the subgroup tier has the lowest marginal cost for
both AEADs ($5.81\times$ and $8.41\times$ over S1 small-footprint). At
200\,MHz the two-core prototype sustains 203\,MB/s AES-GCM and 116\,MB/s
ChaCha20-Poly1305 at S3---0.81 and 0.46\,Gb/s per core---against
2.8 and 17.5\,MB/s in software. Whole-run throughput, which pays the
start-up that marginal figures cancel, appears with the state-placement
analysis below.

\subsection{The subgroup must span the block state}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/fig_width}
\caption{Large-footprint speedup over each algorithm's own S1 for
subgroup-cooperative forms. Four lanes is the right width for AES's 128-bit
state and the wrong width for ChaCha's 512-bit state; at sixteen lanes the
ChaCha result inverts, $1.29\times{\to}4.32\times$ ($8.41\times$
small-footprint).}
\label{fig:width}
\end{figure}
Fig.~\ref{fig:width} isolates the rule. AES-GCM's four-lane form
returns $4.92\times$ because its block state \emph{is} four lanes wide: one
\texttt{aesrm.sg4} holds the whole state, and ShiftRows becomes wiring. The
same four-lane structure applied to ChaCha returns $1.29\times$: a 512-bit
state spans four quads, every quarter-round reads words a \emph{different}
quad holds, and the cross-quad traffic stays in software---its per-byte
DRAM traffic is the worst in the design (140 bytes moved per payload byte
at the small point, against S1's 97), which is why, uniquely, its
small-footprint cost exceeds its large-footprint one. Widening the
subgroup to sixteen lanes---the state's own width---turns the diagonal
permutation into fixed routing inside one instruction, and the same
algorithm returns $4.32\times$ ($8.41\times$ small-footprint). Width is not
acting alone: the sixteen-lane form also raises what one instruction
advances from one ARX line to a full double round, and
Table~\ref{tab:state}'s stateless row isolates that granularity half at
fixed width---the same sixteen-lane layout with line-granular instructions
runs $1.78\times$ slower. Counters add a memory leg: a lane-mapped
kernel walks sixteen unrelated messages per warp and scatters (ChaCha S1:
79 DRAM bytes per payload byte, 1.7\% write hits) where the
matched-width form walks one contiguous block and coalesces (49\,B/B at
39\%; 48 against 9 for AES)---matching the subgroup to the block state
turns sixteen scattered streams into one. Stated as a rule: \emph{a
subgroup-cooperative form pays when the subgroup and the instruction's
granularity together span the cipher's block state; narrower or
finer-grained forms leave the state movement in the instruction stream, and
with it most of the win.} Two ciphers instantiate the rule at $k{=}4$ and
$k{=}16$; it is a property of the block state's extent, not of either
cipher.

\subsection{State placement has an interior optimum}
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Three placements for the state of the ChaCha round instruction,
same kernel, same machine. The middle wins both axes' trade.}
\label{tab:state}
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\input{tables/tab_state}
\end{table}
Table~\ref{tab:state} fixes the algorithm and the sixteen-lane structure and
varies only where the round's state lives. At one end, a stateless
quarter-round-line instruction (the direct analogue of the AES form):
combinational, single-cycle, nothing held anywhere---and $1.78\times$ slower
than the ten-cycle macro, despite executing on the same machine. The
mechanism is issue bandwidth, not latency: it needs $2.88\times$ the
instructions (eighty round instructions per block against ten), and although
the machine runs that stream \emph{better} per instruction (instruction
throughput rises $1.40\times$; scoreboard stall falls from 92\% to 76\%),
the throughput gain cannot pay for a $2.88\times$ instruction count. The latency the macro exposes is nearly
free---doubling the warp count recovers only 12\%, so ten cycles of blocking
were costing at most that---and pipelining the macro to accept one
instruction per cycle is $1.1\%$ \emph{slower} (the unit is 13\% occupied;
the chain is serially dependent). At the other end, the S2 engine holds the
smallest instruction stream in the table (28.9 per block) and still loses to
the macro on cycles---115.6 against 110.6 per 64-byte block large-footprint,
and 90.9 against 56.4 small-footprint---while adding
$2.86\times$ the area and the only resident secrets in the design.
We implement the engines but not preemption save-or-destroy; that
specification burden is itself part of the tier's price, and the middle
point simply does not owe it. \emph{A macro instruction wins by moving work
out of the instruction stream, not by being fast; its working state should
live exactly as long as one instruction.}

The slope is only half the trade; per-message start-up is the other.
Nonce setup, the Poly1305 key block, and tag finalisation cost the engine
${\sim}$0.8k cycles per record, S1 ${\sim}$1.2k, the sixteen-lane macro
${\sim}$8.6k---partly software run sixteen-wide-redundant, partly
mapping (one record per subgroup keeps eight in flight against S1's 128).
Persistent context is, mechanically, start-up amortisation, and the macro
repays it with statelessness: whole-run it overtakes S1 near 1.3\,KiB
records, but against the engine---whose marginal it only ties---the
crossover sits near 100\,KiB, and at 2\,KiB records the engine is
$2.9\times$ faster whole-run. The macro's constituency is long records,
streams, and any deployment unwilling to pay S2's context lifetime; for
short records the engine's amortisation is real, bought with exactly the
resident secrets this section prices.

One inversion in Table~\ref{tab:tiers} now has its explanation: at S3
\emph{both} algorithms retire more instructions than at S2
($2.7\times$ for AES, $1.7\times$ for ChaCha) and both are faster on the
marginal ($2.71\times$ for AES; $1.05\times$ large-footprint and
$1.61\times$ small-footprint for ChaCha). S2 spends area and lifetime semantics to
shrink the instruction stream; S3 spends issue slots to avoid the context
--- and issue slots, unlike resident secrets, are a renewable resource.

\section{Related work}\label{sec:related}
\textbf{CPU cryptography ISEs.} AES-NI~\cite{gueron2010aesni} and RISC-V's
scalar extensions~\cite{riscv-scalar-crypto} define the lane-local
vocabulary; HARE's S1 is their SIMT port, and our measurements quantify
how far it carries ($14.6$--$18.2\times$ for AES, $1.55\times$ for ChaCha). The vector extensions~\cite{riscv-vector-crypto} encode the width
rule for AES (\texttt{vaes*} on 128-bit element groups) but offer ChaCha
no ratified form and no 512-bit group---SIMT subgroups supply exactly
that width, where our sixteen-lane result lives.
\textbf{GPU software cryptography} reaches back to early CUDA
AES~\cite{manavski2007cuda}; such implementations set the S0 bar every
tier here is measured against.
\textbf{GPU confidential computing} puts AEAD on the CPU--GPU path;
recent systems work reduces its \emph{scheduling}
overheads~\cite{wang2024fastrack,lee2025gputee}, orthogonal to---and
composing with---an ISE's per-byte cost reduction.
\textbf{Fixed-function accelerators} deliver bandwidth but freeze the
algorithm and sit outside the SIMT programming model; HARE's tiers are
programmable instructions inside it.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
Four tiers, two AEADs, one machine, everything measured: lane-local
instructions solve AES-GCM's tables and barely touch ChaCha; stateful
engines cost the most and win neither;
subgroup-cooperative instructions carry the lowest marginal cost for
both---provided the subgroup and the instruction's granularity span the
block state, working state lives exactly as long as one instruction, and
records amortise the start-up. The rules are properties of block-state
extent and issue bandwidth, not of these ciphers; what ran out first was
opcode space---budget it as deliberately as ALMs.

\balance
